profile.reading:
Liberty Center One's Royal Oak, Michigan data center at 4815 Delemere Avenue occupies a converted industrial building that the company's own site describes as a former tool and die shop, repurposed into a 21,000 square foot data center in what Liberty Center One calls the heart of Automation Alley, southeast Michigan's cluster of automation, robotics, and advanced manufacturing companies centered on Oakland County. Converting light industrial buildings into data centers is a common pattern in secondary markets, where operators favor existing structures with sturdy floor loading, available power, and lower acquisition cost over ground up construction.

According to Liberty Center One's own published specifications, the facility supports up to 20 kilowatts of power per rack, well above the 3 to 4 kilowatts per rack the company says is typical of commercial colocation space, and delivers what it describes as more than 250 watts of fully redundant power per square foot. Applied across the stated 21,000 square feet, that per square foot figure would put total facility power capacity in the range of several megawatts, though Liberty Center One does not publish a single total megawatt number for the site. The company states the facility runs an N plus N uninterruptible power supply system with diverse power routing, N plus 1 backup generation, diverse fiber building entrances, and a Starline busway system it says can bring new power circuits online within 30 minutes of a customer request, a speed of deployment aimed at colocation and managed hosting customers who need to scale quickly.

Cooling is handled through an ASHRAE managed system with free cooling economization, taking advantage of Michigan's cold season to reduce mechanical cooling load, backed by an inert gas fire suppression system rather than water based suppression, a choice common in facilities protecting active electronic equipment. Liberty Center One states the facility maintains SSAE 16 SOC 1 and SOC 2 compliance along with ISO, HIPAA, and PCI standards, verified through regular third party audits, and describes its network as built on a fully redundant Cisco core with diverse internet service provider connections offering full gigabit redundancy. The company references Tier 3 level capabilities for uptime, though the site does not show a formal Uptime Institute certification. Detailed tenant information and the exact date of the industrial to data center conversion are not published.
profile.research_note: Expansion pass 2026-09-04: per libertycenterone.com/data-centers/, this building is described by the operator as a converted former tool and die shop (21,000 sqft), not a former Sears store as sometimes assumed. Could not corroborate or refute a Sears-building origin via county property records or trade press this session (Crain's Detroit 403, Data Center Frontier article did not cover this property, Oakland County GIS page not found at guessed URL). Wrote reading strictly from what the operator's own current site states (tool and die shop) rather than repeating unverified lore. Added specs: 20kW/rack, 250W/sqft redundant power, N+N UPS, N+1 generator, Starline busway 30-min deployment, ASHRAE free cooling, inert gas suppression, SSAE-16 SOC1/SOC2, ISO/HIPAA/PCI, Cisco redundant mesh network, "Tier 3" capability language (not a certified Tier rating).

reading.body:
Liberty Center One sits in Royal Oak, Michigan, with no published power capacity, square footage, or facility certifications on the operator's homepage. The facility has been mapped and its address verified, but the figures necessary to assess its scale or purpose remain unpublished.

Michigan has six mapped data center facilities across the state, yet none publish megawatt capacity on their operator spec pages. Liberty Center One ranks first by published capacity in Michigan only because all other facilities in the state also publish zero figures. This ranking reflects absence of disclosure rather than superiority.

Without published power specifications, the site's relevance to AI infrastructure cannot be determined from available data. An operator choosing not to disclose capacity typically signals either that the facility serves purposes other than large-scale compute, or that publication would not serve the operator's business interests. Readers assessing AI's grid constraint should note this facility as unmeasured rather than as part of Michigan's data center footprint.
